name: Critique of the subject-predicate logic underlying holism
plain_explanation: Russell traces Hegel's whole system to an error in traditional logic: the assumption that every true statement must be of the form 'a thing has a property,' which cannot properly handle relations between two or more things (like 'John is the father of James') and so (mistakenly) seems to force everything back into statements about one all-encompassing Whole.
precise_definition: The claim, which Russell attributes as implicit in Hegel's system (though not explicit in Hegel's own texts), that traditional subject-predicate logic -- which treats every fact as a single subject having a single property -- cannot accommodate relational facts (like 'A and B are two,' or 'John is the father of James') except by relocating the truth of such statements to 'the Whole,' since relations involve two or more things rather than one.
why_it_mattered: For Russell, this is the technical root of Hegel's entire metaphysics of the Absolute: 'the worse your logic, the more interesting the consequences to which it gives rise.'
historical_origin: Reconstructed by Russell as implicit in Hegel's system and in that of other metaphysicians who share a similar outlook.
examples: 'Uncle' as a relational predicate: a man can become an uncle without any change in his own intrinsic qualities, which subject-predicate logic struggles to accommodate
Russell's demonstration that if Hegel were right, no word could have a meaning, since fully specifying 'John' would require already knowing the meanings of all other words in the universe
competing_positions: Modern relational logic (developed by Russell himself elsewhere), which treats relations as genuinely real without requiring reduction to a single Whole
influence_on_later_thinkers: Represents an early statement of Russell's broader project (with Moore) of refuting British Idealism through the logic of relations.
